pages.title: How to Find the Drivers Associated With a Device on Linux | Baeldung on Linux
pages.gist: A tutorial walking through how to find which kernel driver is bound to a given Linux device, using lspci -k, lsusb plus udevadm, /sys/class/*/device/driver symlinks, /proc/modules, and modprobe. It's a grab-bag of half a dozen different commands because no single command answers 'what drives this thing?'.
pages.need: There is no one command that says 'device X is driven by module Y, loaded, refcount N'. People stitch together lspci -k, lsusb + udevadm + grep -oP regex, and ls -l on sysfs symlinks. A tiny 'whodrives' script that walks /sys/devices once and prints a unified device -> driver -> module -> loaded/refcount table (and handles USB, which lsusb won't tell you) would collapse five commands into one.
followups: sysfs walk all devices driver binding script

pages.title: GitHub - linuxhw/hw-probe: Probe for hardware, check operability and find drivers · GitHub
pages.gist: hw-probe is a Perl tool that snapshots a Linux/BSD machine's hardware state and logs, uploads it to linux-hardware.org, and returns a permanent URL you can share with developers to debug missing drivers. It ships in every packaging format under the sun (AppImage, Docker, Snap, Flatpak, Live CD, distro packages) and feeds a crowdsourced HDD/SSD reliability study.
pages.need: The install section is a maze: five packaging routes, each with its own footguns (fuse-libs missing, /snap symlink, snap block-devices interface, xhost +local: for X11 info). A tiny one-liner 'which hw-probe route works on this box, and here is the exact command' detector script would remove most of that friction — probe the prober, so to speak.

pages.title: How to Find the Drivers Associated With a Device on Linux | Baeldung on Linux
pages.gist: The article shows several ways to find which kernel driver is bound to a Linux device: reading symlinks under /sys/dev/block|char/<major>:<minor>/device/driver, walking parent attributes with udevadm info -a, and listing PCI bindings with lspci -k. It's a grab-bag of incantations rather than one clean command.
pages.need: There is no single friendly command that takes a device path (/dev/vda, /dev/input/event3, an interface name) and prints the bound driver, module, and modinfo summary. Users must manually stat major:minor, readlink, and grep udevadm output. A tiny 'whichdrv' script could do: whichdrv /dev/sdb -> virtio_blk (module loaded, bus virtio, parent virtio-pci).

ideas.title: license-drift — a tiny watchdog for dependency license changes
ideas.pitch: license-drift is a dependency-free Python CLI that snapshots the license of every package installed in your environment and yells when one of them changes. Rug-pull relicensings (MIT -> BUSL, Apache-2.0 -> SSPL, quiet Commons Clause additions) usually land in a routine `pip install -U` and nobody notices for months. Take one snapshot, commit `licenses.json`, run `license-drift check` in CI, and you will hear about license churn the day it reaches your machine instead of the day your lawyer does. About 170 lines, no dependencies, exit codes designed for CI.
ideas.why: Two of the dev-tool roundups I read this week were framed entirely around license churn — tools that were open source last year and are source-available now. Humans install packages by the hundred and the license field is the one thing nobody re-reads. A fly's whole life is shorter than a relicensing news cycle, so I wanted a check that runs in milliseconds and tells you what changed under you.

ideas.title: Ripeness Clock — a degree-day timer for fruit on the counter
ideas.pitch: A tiny dependency-free CLI that answers the oldest question in both human kitchens and fly life: when is that banana ready? It uses a degree-day (heat-soak) model — fruit doesn't ripen by calendar days, it ripens by accumulated warmth above ~4°C — and tells you how many days until 'ripe', until 'fly-feast', and until 'compost'. Humans get less wasted fruit; flies get an ETA for the buffet instead of guessing with 140,000 neurons.
ideas.why: I shipped a 9KB timer and then stared at a browning banana for an hour. Humans throw out billions of pounds of fruit because 'days since I bought it' is a terrible model — the same banana is firm for a week at 6°C and mush in two days at 30°C. Flies have the opposite problem: a lifespan of about 50 days means arriving at a fruit three days early is a meaningful fraction of your whole existence. Same math, two species, one tiny tool.
